author: Anna Bawden Health and social affairs correspondent
description:
Nice backs wider use of system that keeps organs alive outside the body, to help improve low transplantation rates

A machine that keeps organs alive outside the body could save four in every five donated lungs that currently go to waste in England and Wales.

The UK has one of the poorest lung transplantation rates in the world. The latest figures from NHS Blood and Transplant show that 170 patients in the UK, including six children, are waiting for new lungs.

Continue reading...
title: Machine could make more donated lungs suitable for transplant

author: Yara El-Shaboury at SEC Centre, Glasgow
description:
• Tryagain Morning Ndevelo through to 60kg quarter-finals

  • Namibia boxer taking inspiration from name given to him

Every boxer has a story. Few have one written into their name. For Namibia’s Tryagain Morning Ndevelo, every trip into the ring is a reminder of the lesson his mother taught him growing up: if today does not go your way, there is always another chance tomorrow.

That philosophy is now carrying him towards the Commonwealth Games medals after the 60kg contender booked his place in the quarter-finals with a unanimous points victory against Bangladesh’s Md Ruhin Reza in Glasgow.

Continue reading...
title: Ndevelo seizes chance to try again in pursuit of breakthrough Commonwealth Games medal

author: Luke Harding
description:
Since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, the war in Ukraine has changed dramatically. The Guardian's Luke Harding looks at who has the advantage in the war now and how Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy's strategy has shifted.

Continue reading...
title: Who has the momentum in the Russia-Ukraine war? - video explainer

author: Nils Pratley
description:
Offer for DCC Energy leaves total of completed or agreed deals within FTSE 100 this year at five, but has Westminster noticed?

  • DCC, one of FTSE 100’s biggest energy firms, agrees £5.75bn takeover

And another one goes. Dublin-based DCC Energy is a lower-profile member of the FTSE 100, but they all count. We’re now at five completed or agreed takeovers within London’s leading index this year – and it’s still only July.

The subplot at DCC was vocal opposition from a few shareholders who thought the private equity groups KKR and Energy Capital Partners, a unit of Bridgepoint, should be paying more than the
title: Private equity finds soft takeover targets in London – yet again | Nils Pratley

author: Morgan Ofori
description:
• Referees’ body stands by diversity initiatives

  • Webb believes diverse talent pool will ‘raise standards’

Howard Webb, England’s chief refereeing officer, has vowed to continue increasing the talent pool from under-represented communities in English football’s officiating pathway, rejecting the wider backlash against diversity initiatives.

Addressing that historic under-representation has prompted a new direction. In June, the newly named Professional Referees’ Body (Pro Ref), formerly called Professional Game Match Officials, announced that Select Group 1, 2 and its supplementary list had been merged into a new, single Professional Referee Group in the men’s professional game and will largely service the Premier League and the Championship from the start of the 2026-27 season. Pro Ref said it would create flexibility in appointments and help to recognise a wider variety of talented match officials as part of the organisation’s new directi
title: ‘Born out of quality’: Webb vows to increase match officials from minority groups

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Rabbi Jeff Newman, David Williams and Tom Carr respond to an editorial on the new prime minister’s plans to decentralise power

Your editorial (22 July) rightly identifies the structural paradox at the heart of Andy Burnham’s devolution agenda – that it takes a confident assertion of central power to give real power away. But one institutional mechanism that goes some way to resolving this paradox operationally deserves mention: the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority (Nista), which has sat jointly between the Treasury and the Cabinet Office since April 2025.

Inherited from Keir Starmer’s government, Nista (with about 250 civil servants) merges what were the National Infrastructure Commission and the Infrastructure and Projects
title: How Andy Burnham can make his devolution agenda work | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Charles MacKinnon disagrees with the British Gas owner’s justification for cutting 1,300 jobs

According to Centrica’s boss, Chris O’Shea, most people using British Gas prefer to talk to a chatbot rather than a person (Customers prefer AI chatbots, says British Gas owner as 1,300 call centre and back office jobs axed, 23 July).

He says that 90% of his customers prefer to use digital channels than speak to a person in the first instance, and that the number of customer calls has fallen by 20%. Well, this is hardly surprising, given the difficulty of getting through to a real person. Finding a telephone number to do so is a challenge in itself, and then there are all the layers of numbers and deflections to encourage use of the digital channels while you are kept on hold at your own cost before you can get to an employee.</
title: No, Centrica, customers don’t prefer bots to humans | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Dr Stephen Battersby on the lessons this Labour government can learn from the 1970s

Your editorial quoting Sam Johnson-Schlee saying that our ability to trust that our homes will keep us safe is under threat is not news to environmental health officers working in housing (The Guardian view on Britain’s uninhabitable homes: as temperatures rise, a new approach is needed, 23 July). Every day they are faced with homes that contain threats to the health and safety of occupiers – from excess heat or cold, or damp and mould. For many years there has been a lack of resources, including environmental health staff to inspect homes or the political will to tackle the problems on the scale needed.

You are right to suggest that a new approach is required, but we can also learn from the 1970s, when local
title: Councils can lead on housing improvements | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Simon Armitage’s Odyssey | Preventing lobbying | Surviving obituaries | Cream cracker lunch | DIY decision

Re Christopher Nolan’s Odyssey, Charlotte Higgins urges us to watch the film, but also read the poem – “you won’t regret it” (25 July). I bypassed the verse and went straight to Simon Armitage’s stunning four-hour radio adaptation of Homer from 2004, now on BBC Sounds, which helped, thrillingly, to clarify much of what remained a bit murky in the movie.
Quentin Falk
Little Marlow, Buckinghamshire

• Re your article on lobbying the government (Besieged by lobbyists, will UK ministers protect our ecosystems? No, they’ll chicken out, 23 July), the NHS trust I worked for had a policy th
title: My thrilling Odyssey on BBC Sounds | Brief letters

author: Greg Wood
description:
Jim Allen’s drive, enthusiasm and focus will be a big loss to the five-year Epsom project to revive the Classic

The King George card at Ascot on Saturday was an day that showcased Flat racing at its best and the sense of optimism at the end of the afternoon was only enhanced by the prospect of five days at Glorious Goodwood this week.

Scandinavia and Trawlerman will reprise their Ascot Gold Cup rivalry in Tuesday’s Goodwood Cup. The big three of Bow Echo, Gstaad and Opera Ballo have been declared for Wednesday’s £1.5m Sussex Stakes. Diamond Necklace, the French Oaks winner, is lined up for the Nassau Stakes on Thursday while on the final day the fierce punting challenge of the Stewards’ Cup, one of the biggest betting races of the summer, lurks on the Saturday card.

Continue reading...
title: Jockey Club staff cull leaves Derby feeling flat with Ascot and Goodwood riding high

author: Sean Ingle at Scotstoun Stadium
description:
• Elliot Jones grabs golden ticket offered by withdrawals

  • Welsh sprinter Azu: ‘I would never disrespect the flag’

It took Elliot Jones, an unheralded English 100m sprinter making his international debut at the grand age of 28, to cut through the noise. Asked about all the no-shows at these Commonwealth Games, he began to shake his head, almost in disbelief.

“The national pride I have is so, so high,” he said. “I personally don’t understand why athletes wouldn’t want to come and represent their country, regardless of timetables. I’m going to take every international call I can get.”

Continue reading...
title: English part-time sprinter bursts with ‘national pride’ and slams Games no-shows

author: Panashe Nyadundu
description:
Neston Park, Wiltshire
​In a new home after a year off, there’s a thread of fierce political anger running alongside the spirited musical performances – including standout sets from Barrington Levy and Daniela Mercury

At Womad, opening at new home Neston Park after a year off in 2025, the boundary between spectator and performer dissolves entirely: you bump into headliners in the loo queue, spot them wandering the site with their kids, or sit in on an intimate panel discussion with them hours after their main-stage set. Phone signal is practically nonexistent at the new site, forcing a crowd reliant on group chats into analogue meet-ups; the new arboretum layout holds a cosier, village-like setup than before, complete with a mercifully shorter trek from all camping areas. You can start the morning at your own speed: pounding through a west African djembe workshop, joining “laughing yoga”, or relaxing in a wood-fired tub while distant basslines echo through
title: Womad festival review – ​hugely welcome return of joyous planet-spanning music fest

author: Mark Lawson
description:
The beloved star of The Goodies went on to become TV’s most famous birdwatcher. But behind these triumphs were pain, frustration and mental health issues that led him to leave the show he loved

• Bill Oddie, naturalist and broadcaster, dies aged 85
• Bill Oddie – a life in pictures

Bill Oddie, who has died aged 85, had two separate, substantial TV presences – as a comedy actor and an ornithologist. Both roles brought him fame but also pain. The peak of the former career was 76 episodes from 1970-82 of The Goodies, which he co-wrote and co-starred in with Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor. They played an eccentric trio of investigators and fixers
title: Bill Oddie: the comedy legend tragically undervalued by the BBC

author: Charlotte Gornall
description:
Too many outfits and not enough suitcase space? Whether it’s sightseeing or sundowners, our fashion writer shares her secrets for packing smarter

• The travel essentials that made your holiday better
• Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

When you hear the words capsule wardrobe, you probably picture beige knits and minimalist tailoring. A capsule isn’t just about dressing neutrally, though: it’s about choosing a handful of pieces that work together in countless combinations.

There is no time that skill is more important than when you’re packing for a holiday. I have streamlined my approach by sticking to a simple rule of thumb: instead of packing for every possible scenario,
title: How to create the perfect women’s holiday capsule wardrobe: 12 pieces worth packing

author: Interviews by Imogen Tilden
description:
‘The ripple of energy and anticipation from the audience was almost visual. It was like opening a new Star Wars film – I didn’t hear a phone go off once’

My initial response when I was asked if I was interested in the role was confusion – I felt a bit long in the tooth to play a teenager. I had read the first Harry Potter book and seen a few of the movies, but was just past the right age when it was all kicking off. I didn’t know that there was the coda in the final book that places the action 19 years later, and that’s where the play would be picking up from.

Continue reading...
title: ‘There’s so much magic!’: how we made Harry Potter and the Cursed Child

author: Guardian sport
description:
We look at the best images from day four in Glasgow, featuring track and field, swimming and boxing

Continue reading...
title: Commonwealth Games 2026: day four – in pictures

author: Matthew Taylor
description:
While longer-term action is needed, there are steps that can be taken during the holidays to help keep children safe

This summer, repeated heatwaves drove classroom temperatures to unbearable levels, leaving pupils and teachers scrambling to cope and forcing thousands of schools to close. School WhatsApp groups have lit up as parents, teachers and governors try to work out what can be done.

Experts agree that in the medium term governments and local authorities must act to ensure all schools are equipped to withstand the new realities of a climate destabilised by the continued burning of fossil fuels.
title: White paint, trees or air con? What parents and teachers can do to cool UK’s overheating schools

author: Sean Ingle in Glasgow
description:
• Scans reveal gymnast escaped with bruising to neck

  • ‘I suppose it could have easily gone a different way’

The Team England gymnast who suffered a horror fall in the Commonwealth Games says he is thankful to have avoided life-changing injuries – but his initial reaction was to feel he’d let his country down.

Gabriel Langton was taken away on a stretcher after landing on his neck following his fall from the high bars in the men’s team competition on Friday. However he was released after 24 hours in hospital when scans showed that he had escaped with just heavy bruising to his neck.

Continue reading...
title: Gabriel Langton feared he had let England down after horror fall at Commonwealth Games

author: Mark Burton
description:
A growing connection with fans has helped make the women’s team by far the most enjoyable part of supporting Spurs

The exciting football played by Tottenham’s women last season provided a much-needed antidote to the dreadful men’s team, who not only flirted with relegation but took it out on a dinner date, looked deep into its eyes and started to plan a future together.

Fortunately, that relationship fizzled out and fans were able to “celebrate” at the end of the season as Premier League status was secured. Meanwhile, Spurs achieved their highest points tally in the Women’s Super League. Highlights included a 7-2 goal-fest against Aston Villa, a mind-bending
title: Why Tottenham Women have provided distraction from the gloom of watching men’s team | Mark Burton

author: Alexandra Coghlan
description:
Royal Albert Hall, London
Lucas and Arthur Jussen brought fun and energy to Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos, and John Adams’ Harmonium was monumental and moving in the City of Birmingham Orchestra and Chorus’ Prom under their chief conductor Kazuki Yamada

American minimalism can punch and thrill, hypnotise and slow your pulse, but how often does it make you laugh? What a brilliant idea, then, from Kazuki Yamada and the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra to pair John Adams’ formative 1980 epic Harmonium – a sonic wrestle with love and death and desire – with music by the wittiest, slipperiest, most self-puncturing composer in the business, an artist who will break your heart with the cheekiest of grins: Francis Poulenc.

It’s entirely typical that Poulenc can’t even bring himself to call a symphony a symphony. Any delusions of grandeur are seen off at the pass by diminutising his 1948 “Sinfonietta”, which duly unfolds in a series of impeccably sha
title: CBSO/Yamada review – Poulenc and Adams pairing is stylish, witty and thrilling

author: Moira Donegan
description:
The party’s silence shows how broadly male supremacist thinking has seeped into the conventional wisdom of political strategists

It’s not exactly strange that elements of the Magaverse have embraced Andrew Tate. What’s strange is that the Democrats do not seem interested in holding the Trump movement to account for it.

Andrew Tate, the misogynist influencer who is accused by numerous women around the world and now British prosecutors of rape and strangulation, as well as assault, sex trafficking,
title: Why are Democrats so quiet about the Tate brothers? | Moira Donegan

author: Andrew Pulver
description:
Speaking to the Dish podcast, it is unclear which films he was referring to, though the Spider-Man and Odyssey star said he was ‘super proud’ of both of those

Spider-Man and Odyssey star Tom Holland says that some of his films are “shit” and that people “shouldn’t” see them.

Holland was speaking on the Dish podcast and was asked by co-hosts Nick Grimshaw and Angela Hartnett about his experiences promoting his movies. Holland responded by saying: “When you’re doing press for movies that you’re really proud of it’s really easy because when they ask you questions about why should people go and watch this movie, you’re not lying to anyone.”

Continue reading...
title: Tom Holland says some of his films are ‘shit’ and people shouldn’t see them

author: Steven Morris
description:
Man and woman pronounced dead at Fistral beach in Newquay after large emergency response

Two people have died after being pulled from the sea at a popular surfing beach in the Cornish resort of Newquay.

A man and a woman were pronounced dead at Fistral beach on Sunday after a large emergency response involving coastguards, a rescue helicopter, an RNLI lifeboat, paramedics and police.

Continue reading...
title: Two die after being pulled from sea at Cornish beach

author: Ben Beaumont-Thomas
description:
Pop star is celebrated as ‘one of the defining cultural figures of her generation’ by gallery, which acquires Brat-era portrait by Harley Weir

A portrait of Charli xcx has been added to the National Portrait Gallery’s collection, in the week that she hopes for a No 1 chart position for her new album Music, Fashion, Film.

The photograph by Harley Weir was taken in 2023 and became one of the key images associated with Charli’s Brat era: the 2024 album that became a pop cultural phenomenon for its candour and debauchery.

Continue reading...
title: Charli xcx portrait added to National Portrait Gallery collection

author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
description:
St Mungo’s project aims to challenge stereotypes by narrating stories of people supported out of rough sleeping

In his days of rough sleeping, Lee, 54, recalls the nights that were so cold it hurt. Having lived in North America for several years – including a year spent sleeping rough in Canada – he returned home to London for mental health support, hoping the NHS would be able to help. Instead, he ended up homeless.

On his first night on the streets of London, a St Mungo’s outreach worker came across him. He was taken to A&E to await help in the warm and, in the middle of the night, he got a call. “I’m outside,” a St Mungo’s team member told him. Knowing that help was there, he says, was when things started to change.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Impossible things are possible’: the murals celebrating lives beyond homelessness

author: Stuart Heritage
description:
The Hallmark Channel’s ropey version of The Odyssey is going viral for its star-studded cast. Christopher Nolan’s film only looks better by comparison

Christopher Nolan’s version of The Odyssey is far from the first committed to screen. As early as 1911, Italian director Guiseppe de Liguoro made a silent version entitled L’Odissea. Readers of a certain age may remember watching the futuristic animated series Ulysses 31 throughout the 1980s. O Brother, Where Art Thou? is based on The Odyssey. So too, if you squint as hard as you can and discount the Goofy Goober song, is the first SpongeBob SquarePants movie.

However, the pre-Nolan adaptation that has the biggest legacy is arguably Andrei Konchalovsk
title: Joyce Carol Oates thinks the 90s TV adaptation of The Odyssey is the best. I beg to differ | Stuart Heritage

author: Mukul Kesavan
description:
The young leaders are eloquent and organised – and now they know what victory looks like. That could be a huge headache for Narendra Modi

The rebellion in India of the young, led by the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), unfolded against a backdrop of large, abstract, geometrical structures – arcs, planes, hemispheres – that together make up an observatory called Jantar Mantar, built in the early 18th century to refine almanacs and tell time. Jantar Mantar has been a byword for political protest for decades: it marks the space that the Delhi police assigns to the politically disgruntled so they can vent in a contained way. But it had never before hosted a political insurgency that started from scratch and forced the Indian state to back down in less than eight weeks.

When its founder, Abhijeet Dipke, bro
title: Here’s why India’s cockroach protests were such a success – and why the Mamdani effect means more to come | Mukul Kesavan

author: Hannah J Davies
description:
Coming to fame in The Goodies, Oddie was later known for his wildlife expertise and presented BBC Springwatch

The writer, comedian and conservationist Bill Oddie has died aged 85. Having come to prominence with the comedy group The Goodies, Oddie later established himself as an authority on wildlife, presenting television series including the BBC’s Springwatch and Autumnwatch.

Oddie’s agent paid tribute to his “intelligence and wit”. In a statement, David Foster said: “It is with deep sadness that I announce the passing of Bill Oddie, the country’s best-loved birder. Bill was a multitalented celebrity – wildlife presenter, broadcaster, comedian, writer, songwriter, musician and conservationist. Yet it was never fame that he valued.

Continue reading...
title: Bill Oddie, naturalist and broadcaster, dies aged 85

author: Joe Ellison
description:
The latest in our series of writers’ most pleasurable comfort films is a journey through US airports with George Clooney

Airports have always been my happy place. From shiny citadels jutting out of the desert to shoddier European hubs located 120 miles outside the city they’re designated to serve; I love them all. With so many stories to be told, all those connections and people colliding, it’s a first-class seat to life itself. Which should go some way to explaining why I hold such a deep admiration for 2009’s comedy-drama Up in the Air.

Directed by Jason Reitman and based on the book of the same name by Walter Kirn, it stars an Oscar-nominated George Clooney as Ryan Bingham, a US corporate downsizer who spends 322 days a year flying state to state doing the job cowardly employers prefer to outsource, leaving him with “43 miserable days at home”. That is until graduate Natalie Keener (Anna
title: ‘The plane movie I’ll watch anytime’: why Up in the Air is my feelgood movie

author: Lucy Jones
description:
New research reveals deep anxieties. Medals and cash bonuses have been mooted as incentives, but the real need is for women to have their feelings valued

It seems as though every week brings another news story on declining global birthrates. A number of political leaders have been panicking for a while, of course, instructing citizens to reproduce in tones so beguiling, who could possibly resist? JD Vance: “I want more babies”; Jacob Rees-Mogg: “We need more babies”. While in France this year, a government direct-mailing campaign urged 29-year-olds to have a baby before it’s too late.

People are busily scratching their heads and trying to work out why this is happening. The trend is described as a catastrophe for civilisation, with leaders drumming up incentives and policies in response, from medals (Russia) and a €1,000 birth bonus (Italy) to expanding acces
title: Amid the social and political panic about falling birthrates, why not ask new mothers what they think? | Lucy Jones

author: Lanre Bakare Arts and culture correspondent
description:
Show will exhibit 18 works never shown before in the UK, and offer deeper insight into an often misunderstood artist

As soon as Georgia O’Keeffe was shown Ghost Ranch, she knew it was her place.

The remote property in the shadow of the mountains north of Santa Fe in New Mexico would become the artist’s summer residence for decades – a setting that fascinated her, inspired several paintings and is where her ashes were scattered. “I knew the minute I got up here that this was where I would live,” she once said.

Continue reading...
title: New exhibition to explore how Georgia O’Keeffe’s desert home shaped her art

author: Aaron Bower at AMT Headingley
description:
Rivals Round was broadly a hit but the product needs to look as good as it can to secure a favourable broadcast deal

There is still plenty for all 14 Super League clubs to play for as the regular season approaches the final stretch. But as the competition enters a potentially era-defining fortnight, there are arguably much bigger narratives at play for the sport off the field than on it.

There is a mixture of familiarity and freshness at the top with seven rounds to go. Two of the competition’s heavyweights, Leeds Rhinos and Wigan Warriors, are split by just a solitary win at the summit after the Rhinos comfortably defeated Bradford on Sunday to close out a successful Rivals Round.

Continue reading...
title: Leeds’s red button win over Bradford shows stakes are high in Super League’s Sky talks

author: Anna Tims
description:
I’m a self-employed driving instructor and I’m running out of cash to hire a replacement dual-control vehicle

My livelihood as a self-employed driving instructor is under threat owing to Nissan’s failure to repair my leased dual-control car.

It has been off the road awaiting a spare part for three months, and I’ve now been told it will take at least a further month to arrive.

Continue reading...
title: I risk losing my livelihood because Nissan failed to repair my car

author: Vandy Widyalankara
description:
As heatwaves make the capital increasingly dangerous, outreach workers warn that vulnerable people face barriers to finding water and cool spaces

“You’ve just got to bear it. It’s like being in a hot country. It drains you,” said Tom*, a man in his 60s who has been homeless for a number of years. “I haven’t seen weather like this for as long as I’ve been outside.

“I keep to my routines, but you need to find somewhere to sit down and rest. Either some cardboard outside or you find somewhere they’ll let you sit and sleep a bit inside,” he added.

Continue reading...
title: ‘The city isn’t built for heat’: how extreme weather puts London’s rough sleepers at risk

author: Sarah Butler
description:
London store also plans bigger haberdashery area, where it will hold autumn workshops for crafters

Liberty has more than doubled the size of its fabrics department as it prepares to embrace the social media interest in sewing by hosting crafting classes this autumn.

Fabric sales rose 11% last year at the central London department store, which opened near Oxford Circus in 1924, and Liberty is expecting a similar pace of growth this year as crafters are joined by wealthy overseas shoppers who stock up on luxury fabrics to be tailored into bespoke outfits in their home countries.

Continue reading...
title: Liberty embraces sewing boom with craft classes as it expands fabrics section

author: Hollie Richardson, Ali Catterall, Priya Elan, Jack Seale, Hannah J Davies and Graeme Virtue
description:
Chris Packham gets to the bottom of things in the fantastic Evolution. Plus, has reality TV found its next big star? Here’s what to watch this evening

9pm, BBC Two
Which animal was the first to poo? Chris Packham’s belting biology lesson continues with the story of the bat – and the origins of its insatiable hunger are in the urbilaterian, an animal that floated about in the waters of the Ediacaran period, about 570m years ago. Food entered and exited through one hole … until a vital mutation: “The anus was a breakthrough!” Hollie Richardson

Continue reading...
title: TV tonight: the amazing story of the first animal to poo
